summary.text: A white dwarf is a very dense star that packs a mass comparable to the Sun's into a volume the size of Earth.
It shines from residual heat rather than nuclear fusion, and electron degeneracy pressure alone holds it up against gravity.
Stars like the Sun, too light to collapse into a neutron star or black hole, are expected to become white dwarfs.

facts.label: First recognised
facts.value: 40 Eridani B, found to be white in 1910

items.prompt: A friend says a white dwarf must still be burning fuel, or gravity would have crushed it. What is wrong with that?

options.label: It burns fuel too slowly for anyone to notice
Its gravity is too weak to cause any crushing
Crowded electrons resist gravity, so no burning is needed
A hidden companion star constantly refuels it

items.explain: The material no longer undergoes fusion and is supported only by electron degeneracy pressure.

items.prompt: A white dwarf's light begins whitish-blue and shifts toward red over time. What explains this?

options.label: It gradually radiates away its stored heat with no new source
Fusion in its core is slowly switching on
It is moving away from us at high speed
Dust gathering around it filters its light

items.explain: White dwarfs are very hot when they form but cool gradually as they radiate energy, so the radiation lessens and reddens.

items.prompt: A star like the Sun lacks the mass to collapse into a neutron star or a black hole. What end is expected for it?

options.label: It explodes and leaves nothing behind
It shrinks further and becomes a pulsar
It stays a main-sequence star forever
It becomes a white dwarf

items.explain: Stars whose mass is not high enough to collapse into a neutron star or black hole are expected to become white dwarfs.

items.prompt: Bessel saw two bright stars shifting position in a regular cycle. What did he predict was behind it?

options.label: Each was drifting steadily toward Earth
Each had a companion that nobody had yet seen
Each was an illusion made by the telescope
Each was orbited by a lone small planet

items.explain: He used position measurements to predict that Sirius and Procyon had unseen companions; Sirius's was later seen as Sirius B.

items.prompt: Why can a white dwarf pack its matter far more tightly than ordinary matter?

options.label: Its atoms are far smaller than atoms on Earth
Its chemical bonds are stronger and pull atoms closer
It is a plasma of loose nuclei and electrons, not atoms
Its gravity squeezes the empty space out of each nucleus

items.explain: White dwarf material is not atoms joined by chemical bonds but unbound nuclei and electrons, so nothing stops nuclei sitting closer than electron orbitals allow.

items.prompt: Suppose a white dwarf's mass climbs past the theoretical maximum for such stars. What goes wrong?

options.label: Its electrons can no longer push back hard enough against gravity
Its density drops until it swells into an ordinary star
Its crystallised interior melts and the star blows apart
Its heat runs out all at once and it goes dark

items.explain: Beyond the Chandrasekhar limit electron degeneracy pressure cannot support the star.

paragraphs.heading: A Sun squeezed to Earth size
paragraphs.text: A white dwarf is an extremely dense star that holds about as much mass as the Sun in a space the size of Earth. It shines from leftover heat and, in time, from crystallizing, not from nuclear fusion. Stars like the Sun, which are not massive enough to become neutron stars or black holes, are expected to end up as white dwarfs. The closest one known is Sirius B, 8.6 light years away, the smaller member of the Sirius pair.

paragraphs.heading: What holds it up
paragraphs.text: Once a white dwarf has formed, no fusion goes on inside it, so it has no heat source to resist gravity. Instead it is held up only by electron degeneracy pressure, which is why it is so dense. That pressure has a ceiling, the Chandrasekhar limit, about 1.44 times the Sun's mass for a white dwarf that is not spinning. Most observed white dwarfs weigh between 0.5 and 0.7 solar masses.

paragraphs.heading: Packed tight
paragraphs.text: Its matter can be so dense because it is not made of atoms joined by chemical bonds. It is a plasma of loose nuclei and electrons, so nothing stops the nuclei from sitting closer together than in ordinary matter. Read from its light, the message of Sirius B was that its material is 3000 times denser than anything people had met, so that a ton of it would fit in a matchbox.

paragraphs.heading: Slowly fading
paragraphs.text: White dwarfs are very hot when they form and cool slowly as they give off their energy. Their light starts at a high color temperature, then fades and reddens over time. In the end they may get cold enough for their material to crystallize, but they are expected to last for 10³⁸ years.

paragraphs.heading: The first one found
paragraphs.text: The first white dwarf found, 40 Eridani B, belongs to a triple star system. In 1910 three astronomers, Henry Norris Russell, Edward Charles Pickering and Williamina Fleming, found that, though dim, it was of spectral type A, or white. It sat far outside the normal pattern on Russell's chart of brightness against color, and Russell publicly suggested its type might be wrong. Walter Adams confirmed the type on his own in 1914.

paragraphs.heading: The companion of Sirius
paragraphs.text: Friedrich Bessel used position measurements to show that Sirius changed its position periodically, and in 1844 he predicted an unseen companion. On 31 January 1862, Alvan Graham Clark spotted a star near Sirius that no one had seen before, and it was later shown to be the predicted companion. In 1915 Adams announced that its spectrum was similar to that of Sirius itself.

paragraphs.heading: Naming and counting
paragraphs.text: Willem Jacob Luyten coined the name white dwarf in 1922, and Arthur Eddington later made it popular. In 1931 Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar worked out a physical model of these stars; he later won the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics for studying how stars evolve. Eighteen white dwarfs were known by 1939, over a hundred by 1950 and over 2000 by 1999. Since then, the Sloan Digital Sky Survey has turned up over 9000, mostly new ones.
